{"id":"49865950","author":"rahloff","text":"Hi HN, I'm Toby. While working on a research paper earlier this year, I got progressively frustrated with the available LaTeX editors. Most need a paid subscription service to enable proper collaboration, are clunky, and shove distracting non-features in your face. This is why I built Aldine. It is a collaborative LaTeX editor that you can run yourself: two containers, every project as a git repo, and AGPL licensed. Documentation:  https://aldine.dev  You can try it without signing up at  https://demo.aldine.dev  (public and wiped every night, so don't leave your thesis there). Create a project, or drop in a ZIP you downloaded from Overleaf. My co-authors want a super simple and browser-based UX. I want git. On Overleaf's cloud the Git integration is a premium feature, and I got tired of copy-pasting files between the two worlds. In Aldine, a colleague who works in VS Code clones the project, commits and pushes, and the people in the browser pull those commits in with one click. Branches, history with diffs, and GitHub/GitLab/Gitea sync all work from the UI. Smaller things: live cursors (Yjs underneath), warm recompiles in about two seconds, a compiler container with no network access. And as of this week you can also sign in through your own OIDC provider, so Authentik, Keycloak or Authelia all work. There's an MCP connector as well, off by default. Claude can edit, compile and fix, and every edit lands as a git commit you can revert. It's v0.x, with rough edges I know about (no keystroke-level track changes yet, and CJK needs the full TeX Live image) and surely some I don't. How do you and your co-authors handle LaTeX today?\nWhat would Aldine need to do or support before you would consider moving your next paper to it?"}

But most models follow instructions well enough when you prompt it, \"Choose one of the following answers:\", it will follow that 90% of the time. Yesterday, just to prove to a friend that Jev isn't that \"revolutionary\" I extracted some image classification code that Claude had written for my private image organizer that used Qwen3-VL, and stopped the output at a single token, then used the probabilities. Input processing on my GPU was somewhere around 1000ms per image, so not too fast, but each question used the prompt cache, so followups were 100ms-ish. That was my baseline of an untrained, non-optimized single pass classification. It would connect to my llama-server, and use the logprobs for the choices. After that, I had Claude remove llama-server from the solution, and write it directly to the transformers, then I kept prompting it to profile and find more speed. Eventually my \"Decision Engine\" running locally on a trained 1B model got  to just under 85% accuracy across my 500 validation prompts (images and text) not used or derived from the training set, and an 8MB image, with 10 questions with 5 choices per question, got down to just under 500ms. Pure text prompts and questions are below 100ms for 300tokens + 10 questions + 5 choices per question (average). It did better on text than images, just because my training set included 90% text. I'll do more training and validation for images when I get home, but for now, I'm more than happy that I can get a local \"decision engine\" running in 4GB of VRAM and responding in under 30ms for most use cases I've had."}

{"number":97740,"title":"VS Code: plan review pane shows previous plan version when ExitPlanMode is batched with a plan-file write","body":"## Summary

In the VS Code extension, the plan review pane ("Ready for review") can show the **previous** version of the plan when the model writes the plan file and calls `ExitPlanMode` in the same tool batch. The approval result contains the new plan, so the user reviews one plan and approves another.

## Environment

- VS Code 1.139.1 (macOS, arm64)
- Extension `anthropic.claude-code` 2.1.283 (darwin-arm64), with its bundled CLI

## Steps to reproduce

1. In plan mode, let the model revise an existing plan.
2. The model emits a `Write` (or `Edit`) to the plan file **and** `ExitPlanMode` in the same parallel tool batch.
3. Look at the "Ready for review" pane.

## Expected

The pane shows the plan as written by that batch, which is what the user is approving.

## Actual

The pane shows the plan as it was **before** that write. The `ExitPlanMode` result (the "Approved Plan" text) contains the new version, so what was reviewed and what was approved differ.

## Evidence

From `Claude VSCode.log`: the `content` of each `open_markdown_preview` request, compared with the plan on disk at that moment.

| Time | Content sent to pane | Plan on disk | Tool calls |
|---|---|---|---|
| 09:00:51 | previous plan (v0) | v1 | Write + ExitPlanMode, same batch |
| 09:01:41 | v1 | v1 + title edit | Edit + ExitPlanMode, same batch |
| 09:05:31 | v1 + title edit | v2 | Write + ExitPlanMode, same batch |
| 09:09:27 | v2 | v2 ✅ | ExitPlanMode alone |
| 09:13:48 | v2 | v3 | Write + ExitPlanMode, same batch |

The pane lags exactly one version every time the write is batched with `ExitPlanMode`. It's correct when `ExitPlanMode` is sent on its own.

## Suspected cause

`ExitPlanMode`'s `plan` field is injected by `normalizeToolInput` ("The plan content (injected by normalizeToolInput from disk)"), via the plan-file cache. The injection appears to happen before the sibling `Write`/`Edit` in the same batch executes, so the snapshot is stale. The webview then forwards `permissionRequest.inputs.plan` to `openMarkdownPreview`, which renders it as-is.

Possible fixes:

- Resolve `plan` when the permission prompt is shown, after earlier tool calls in the batch have completed.
- Or re-read the plan file when rendering the preview.

## Side note (possibly unrelated)

In the extension host, `shutdown()` sets `planPreviewsDetached = true`, and nothing appears to reset it. It also `detach()`es the open preview panels without disposing them. If the same host object is reused afterwards, `openMarkdownPreview` would return early and leave a stale panel on screen. This didn't cause the case above, because the log shows the requests were received, but it may be worth checking.
"}

The session-create request does carry an `effort_level` in `session_context`, but the `--cloud` launch path computes the effort roughly as:

effort: settingsToCloudEnabled && flags.effort !== undefined

```

So unless the settings-to-cloud forwarding path is enabled, `effort` is `undefined` and `effort_level` is omitted entirely. `--model` has no such gate. It seems `--effort` should be forwarded whenever it is explicitly passed, independent of settings forwarding.

{"number":97733,"title":"[FEATURE] Session-scoped /autocompact: change a running session's window only, with separate main/subagent values","body":"### Preflight Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing requests and this feature hasn't been requested yet (related: #90347, #90212, #86716, #83355, #19470; none asks for a session-only runtime change, see below)
- [x] This is a single feature request (not multiple features)

### Problem Statement

I run several Claude Code sessions at the same time, and they need different auto-compact windows. For example, a long coordinator session needs 600k, while a short investigation session is better off at 200k. I also need to change the window **while a session is running**, once I see how the conversation is going. Today there is no way to do that for one session only:

- `/autocompact <value>` always writes `autoCompactWindow` to `~/.claude/settings.json` (user scope). That changes the default for every future session, and every running session that reloads settings picks it up too.
- `--autocompact <tokens>` and `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` are per session, but only at launch. A running session can't change them: a slash command or a Bash call can't change the environment of the running `claude` process.
- The only workaround is to exit and run `claude -c --autocompact <value>`. That interrupts running background work and subagents.
- The main session and its subagents always share one window (see #90347). A coordinator needs a large window, but workers should compact early.

Checked on Claude Code 2.1.280, Linux.

### Proposed Solution

Add a **session scope** to `/autocompact`, with separate values for the main thread and for subagents.

**Commands**

```
/autocompact session 300k              # main thread of this session only
/autocompact session subagents 150k    # subagents spawned by this session only
/autocompact session off               # disable auto-compact for this session only
/autocompact session reset             # drop the session overrides, fall back to env/flag/settings
/autocompact                           # show effective values for main + subagents and where each comes from
```

`/autocompact <value>` without `session` keeps today's behaviour (it writes user settings), so nothing changes for existing users.

**Rules**

1. **Scope.** A session override applies only to the session where it was set. It is never written to any settings file, and it never affects other running sessions or new ones.
2. **Precedence, highest first:** managed/policy settings (as a cap) → session override → `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` → `--autocompact` → `autoCompactWindow` in settings → model default. A command typed in the running session is the most recent explicit choice, so it wins over the launch-time inputs. Unlike today, `/autocompact session` must not be blocked because the env var is set.
3. **Main vs subagents.** The main thread and subagents are resolved separately. If no subagent value is set anywhere, subagents inherit the main value (today's behaviour). Launch-time equivalents for parity: `--autocompact-subagents <auto|tokens>"}

With `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1`, every Bash tool call fails before the command runs:

```
bwrap: Can't mkdir /root/actions-runner-2/.claude: Permission denied
```

This looks like a variant of #79997 (fixed in 2.1.227) that still occurs on 2.1.281.

### Environment

- Claude Code 2.1.281 (native), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, bubblewrap 0.9.0, `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0`.
- Claude runs as **root**. The cwd is `/root/actions-runner-2/_work/<repo>/<repo>` (a second self-hosted GitHub Actions runner).
- `/root/actions-runner-2` is owned by **uid 1001** with mode 755, as extracted from GitHub's runner tarball. All directories below it are owned by root.

### Cause (from the captured bwrap argv)

The sandbox adds denyWrite entries for `<ancestor>/.claude` (and `.mcp.json`) at every ancestor of the cwd, and for missing paths it adds `--ro-bind /tmp/claude-empty-XXXX <ancestor>/.claude`. bwrap runs with `--unshare-user --cap-drop ALL`. Inside that user namespace, uid 1001 is unmapped, so root has no DAC override on `/root/actions-runner-2` and cannot create the mount-point stub. The stubs under root-owned ancestors (`_work/.claude`, `_work/<repo>/.claude`) are fine.

A minimal bwrap test on the same host shows the same result:

```
bwrap --unshare-pid --unshare-user --cap-drop ALL --ro-bind / / --bind /tmp /tmp \
  --ro-bind /tmp/empty /tmp/t/u1001/.claude true   # fails: Can't mkdir ... Permission denied
# same command with /tmp/t/u0 (owned by root) succeeds
```

### Expected

A missing ancestor stub that cannot be created should not kill every Bash call. For example, the fix from #79997 could also cover ancestors that the process owner cannot write to inside the user namespace, not only root-owned ancestors seen by a non-root user.

### Related

- #79997
- #97730 (the same runner host, where `$HOME/actions-runner` is also denied)

On a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installed with GitHub's default layout (runner in `~/actions-runner`, work folder `~/actions-runner/_work`), every Bash tool call fails before the command runs when `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1`:

```
bwrap: Can't create file at /root/actions-runner/_work/<repo>/<repo>/.git/config.lock: Read-only file system
```

`anthropics/claude-code-action` turns the scrub on whenever `allowed_non_write_users` is set, so review workflows on such runners lose all shell access (including `git diff`) and continue without it.

### Cause (from the captured bwrap argv)

The scrub denyWrite list includes `${HOME}/actions-runner` (and `${HOME}/runners`). In the default self-hosted layout, `GITHUB_WORKSPACE` is inside that directory, so the sandbox emits `--ro-bind /root/actions-runner /root/actions-runner` after the workspace `--bind`. The whole workspace becomes read-only. The next deny entry for the non-existent `<workspace>/.git/config.lock` needs a `/dev/null` stub file, which bubblewrap cannot create on the read-only mount, so bwrap exits.

Relevant argv excerpt:

```
--bind /root/actions-runner/_work/<repo>/<repo> /root/actions-runner/_work/<repo>/<repo>
...
--ro-bind /root/actions-runner /root/actions-runner
--ro-bind /dev/null /root/actions-runner/_work/<repo>/<repo>/.git/config.lock
```

### Reproduction

- Claude Code 2.1.281 (native), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, bubblewrap 0.9.0, running as root, `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0`.
- Runner installed per GitHub's instructions at `/root/actions-runner`, default `_work` folder.
- From the workspace, with `HOME=/root`, `GITHUB_WORKSPACE=<workspace>`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1`, run `claude -p` and have the model call Bash with `git rev-parse HEAD`. I drove it with a local mock Messages API, so no model call is needed to reproduce.

### Expected

When the workspace (or cwd) is inside a runner install path, the sandbox should write-protect the runner's own files (`bin`, `externals`, `.runner`, `.credentials`, `_diag`, and so on) and leave the workspace writable, or it should fail with a clear message at startup. Today every Bash call fails, and the run continues silently.

### Related

- #79997 (ancestor denyWrite stubs, fixed in 2.1.227). A second failure on the same runner host, which may be a regression of that fix, is filed separately.

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this hasn't been reported yet
- [x] This is a single bug report (please file separate reports for different bugs)
- [x] I am using the latest version of Claude Code

### What's Wrong?

Switching sessions with `/resume <id>` inside a running Claude Code doesn't reload CLAUDE.md or the auto-memory index (`MEMORY.md`). The resumed session's instructions context stays whatever was captured before:

- **The resumed transcript already has an instructions block:** no new block is added, so the old copy stays in context.
- **The resumed transcript has none**, e.g. one written by a PreCompact hook that forks the conversation: the first message stores the running process's copy, taken at that process's first turn, rather than the files on disk.

Starting with `claude --resume <id>`, or running `/clear`, re-reads both files and stores a fresh instructions block. So the three ways into a session disagree.

The "…changed on disk since you last read it" notices partly cover for this. For the edits I tested (up to a ~22 KB CLAUDE.md rewrite and a ~13 KB MEMORY.md rewrite), the notice carried the diff and the model answered from it. But the stale copy stays in context beside the notice. And in one real session, the notice for a rewritten ~16 KB `MEMORY.md` carried no diff:

```
…/memory/MEMORY.md changed on disk since you last read it. … The changes are not shown here; use Read if you need the current content.
```

That session's instructions held the old index (158 entries, 58 of them pointing at memory files that had since been deleted) plus that one-line hint.

### What Should Happen?

`/resume` inside a running session should reload CLAUDE.md files and the auto-memory index the way `claude --resume` and `/clear` already do, so the resumed session's instructions match the files on disk at the moment of the switch.

### Error Messages/Logs

No error. The evidence is in the session transcript (`~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl`): the instructions attachment is the line containing `Contents of …/CLAUDE.md` and `Contents of …/MEMORY.md`.

### Steps to Reproduce

No plugins needed. `<project>` is the folder's absolute path with every non-alphanumeric character replaced by `-`. Use a folder that isn't inside a git repo.

1. Create `~/cc-resume-repro`. Put `- MEMMARK: four` as the first line of `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md`.
2. In that folder, run `claude -p "Reply OK" --output-format json` and note the `session_id` (call it S). Its transcript stores an instructions block containing `four`.

{"number":97705,"title":"[FEATURE] Remote Control: "Send now" on a queued message should not kill running background agents and tasks","body":"### Preflight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing requests](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20label%3Aenhancement) and this feature hasn't been requested yet
- [x] This is a single feature request (not multiple features)

### Problem Statement

When I drive a session through Remote Control (claude.ai web and mobile) and the session is busy, my message gets queued. Tapping "Send now" on the queued message interrupts the turn, and that interrupt also stops every background agent and background task that is running at the time. So pushing one short message through right away throws away the work of all running agents, often a long test run or several agents in parallel.

### Proposed Solution

"Send now" on a queued message should deliver the message right away but leave running background agents and background tasks alone. Only Stop should end them. The terminal already works this way since 2.1.281: its send-now key moves running work to the background instead of cancelling it (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/interactive-mode#when-claude-code-sends-what-you-queued). Remote Control's "Send now" should do the same.

### Alternative Solutions

Leaving the message queued avoids the kill, because a queued message is handed over at the next tool-call boundary without an interrupt. But it can lag several tool calls behind (#92899), which is why "Send now" exists. A setting to choose between queueing and interrupting (#87656) would also help, but the default for "Send now" should not kill background work.

### Priority

High - Significant impact on productivity

### Feature Category

Other

### Use Case Example

1. From the phone, the session is running four background agents that each run a long test suite.
2. While the main turn is busy, I type a correction and it gets queued.
3. I tap "Send now" so the correction reaches the session immediately.
4. Today: all four agents are killed and their work is lost. Expected: the correction is delivered and the four agents keep running.

### Additional Context

Sessions run through `claude remote-control`, currently on 2.1.280. Related: #95211 (Stop from Remote Control killed four background agents), #78151 and #83024 (an interrupt silently kills background agents), #87656 (setting for queue vs interrupt), #92899 (steering a running task is slow or destructive).
"}

{"number":97703,"title":"[BUG] VS Code: archiving the open session resumes the next one, so archiving N idle sessions leaves N new claude processes running","body":"## Summary

In the VS Code extension, archiving the session that is open in the panel makes the panel open the next session in the list, and opening it **resumes** it: a new `claude` process starts for a session that had none. Archiving that one does not stop its process, and it opens and resumes the next one. Archiving idle sessions one after another therefore starts one process per archived session, and none of them exits.

Archiving 51 sessions over two minutes left 49 new idle `claude` processes of about 230 MiB RSS each (about 11.5 GiB). They stayed alive, with no child processes, until killed by hand.

## Environment

- Claude Code VS Code extension 2.1.283 (native binary, `--output-format stream-json`)
- VS Code 1.139.1, Remote-SSH to a Linux host (Debian 13, kernel 6.12)
- Remote Control connected: each process reattaches to a persisted bridge session
- 55 past sessions in the project

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open a project with many past, idle sessions (no `claude` process running for them).
2. In the Claude panel, archive the open session. The panel opens the next session in the list.
3. Archive that one too, and repeat.
4. Count processes: `ps -eo args | grep -c 'native-binary/claude .*--resume='`

## Expected

- Archiving a session starts no process.
- A process that is running for an archived session is stopped.

## Actual

Each archive is followed by a transcript open and a `launch_claude` with `resume` for the next session. No webview message closes or stops any channel. From `exthost*/Anthropic.claude-code/Claude VSCode.log`, with session ids replaced:

20:57:43.252 webview → launch_claude        resume=<C> freshStartIfUnresumable=false
…
```

{"number":97701,"title":"claude-bin --channels churns sessions and repeatedly kills the plugin MCP server (2.1.283 regression)","body":"**Environment:** macOS 27.0 (headless Mac mini), Claude Code 2.1.283, telegram channel plugin v0.0.7 (`bun server.ts` over stdio).

The plugin's stdio server sees stdin EOF and self-exits, so the channel stops polling until something respawns it. On 2.1.177 the same setup held a single persistent session and MCP connection for weeks.

**Evidence** (MCP logs under `~/Library/Caches/claude-cli-nodejs/-/mcp-logs-plugin-telegram-telegram/`): repeated cycles of `Successfully connected` -> `Channel notifications registered` -> `Cleared connection cache for reconnection` -> `MCP server process exited cleanly`, each with a different `sessionId`. **Expected:** In `--channels` daemon mode the session and its MCP connections should persist for the lifetime of the process.

**Actual:** Session and MCP connection are recycled every couple of minutes, making a channel plugin unusable as a persistent listener.

**Workaround:** roll the daemon back to 2.1.177, or run an external supervisor that restarts the daemon when the MCP child dies.

{"number":97697,"title":"[Desktop/Windows] Tray icon invisible (black on black) when taskbar is dark but app mode is light","body":"**App:** Claude Desktop 2.9939.2.0 (MSIX, x64)
**OS:** Windows 10 Pro 22H2 (10.0.19045)

## Summary

The notification-area icon renders as a black spark on the black taskbar, making it effectively invisible, whenever Windows uses a dark taskbar with light app mode (the Windows 10 "Custom" color mode).

## Steps to reproduce

1. Settings > Personalization > Colors > Choose your color: **Custom**.
2. Default Windows mode: **Dark**. Default app mode: **Light**.
3. Leave Claude's theme set to **System**.
4. Launch Claude and look at the notification area.

**Expected:** White spark (`Tray-Win32-Dark.ico`), visible on the dark taskbar.
**Actual:** Black spark (`Tray-Win32.ico`) on the dark taskbar, so the icon can't be seen.

Registry state:
```
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Themes\Personalize
  AppsUseLightTheme    = 1
  SystemUsesLightTheme = 0
```

## Root cause

The tray icon is picked from the app theme, not the taskbar theme (`app.asar`, minified):

```js
case "ico": return !e && nativeTheme.shouldUseDarkColors ? "Tray-Win32-Dark.ico" : "Tray-Win32.ico";
```

`nativeTheme.shouldUseDarkColors` follows `AppsUseLightTheme` (and Claude's own theme setting). The taskbar colors come from `SystemUsesLightTheme`. When these two differ, Claude shows the wrong icon.

## Suggested fix

- On Windows, choose the tray icon from `SystemUsesLightTheme`, and pick the icon again when that value changes (`WM_SETTINGCHANGE` / "ImmersiveColorSet").
- Or ship a tray icon that shows up on both light and dark taskbars (for example, a white spark on an orange background).

## Why workarounds are not acceptable

- Setting Claude's theme to Dark, or Windows app mode to Dark, changes the look of the app or of every app.
- Making the taskbar light changes the whole desktop.
- The icon files can't be replaced, because the MSIX install folder is read-only and gets replaced on each update.

"}

{"number":97696,"title":"Background subagent reports "completed" with a live Monitor; the Monitor's event never resumes it (still present in 2.1.283, re-filing #86085)","body":"#86085 was closed as stale on 2026-09-10 without a fix. It still reproduces on Claude Code 2.1.283 (macOS), with a minimal case.

## Repro

1. From the main session, launch a background subagent (`Agent` tool, `run_in_background: true`) with this instruction: arm a `Monitor` on `until [ -f $D/flag ]; do sleep 0.5; done; echo "flag detected"` (timeout 10 min), and when it fires, write `$D/seen` and reply `SAW FILE`.
2. The subagent arms the Monitor. The tool result says: "Monitor started (task …, expires in 10m …). You will be notified on each event. Keep working — do not poll or sleep."
3. After about 2 minutes, create `$D/flag` from the parent.

## Expected

The Monitor's event resumes the subagent. It writes `$D/seen`, and the parent gets its final report.

## Actual

- **Early "completed":** 24 s after launch, before the flag existed, the parent got a `completed` task notification for the subagent. Its note said: "This agent stopped with background work of its own still running. It may resume on its own when that work completes or reports, and the same task-id notifies again if it does."
- **Event dropped:** the flag was created at 21:32:37. As of 21:55, 22 minutes later, `$D/seen` doesn't exist, and the parent has had no further notification for that task-id. The parent session sat idle for most of that time, so a busy parent turn isn't the cause.

So the "may resume on its own" path the notice describes doesn't happen, at least when the subagent's pending background work is a Monitor.

## Impact

A parent treats the subagent as finished while the thing it was waiting for is lost. Nothing errors. The harness's own guidance ("do not poll or sleep", use Monitor) leads straight into this path for any long external wait (CI, a file, another process).

## Workaround

Keep long waits in the main session, not in a background subagent, and check any subagent "completed" against the result on disk.
"}

{"number":97694,"title":"[FEATURE] Global "pause all routines" switch to prevent a catch-up burst of missed runs on app launch","body":"**Problem Statement:**
When the desktop app has been closed for a while, every scheduled task (Routine) that missed its slot catches up at once on next launch — I have multiple routines, and booting the app after some downtime started all of them simultaneously. That's a real problem when I'm intentionally low on token budget: I didn't choose to spend usage on N routine runs at that moment, the app did, just because I opened it. There's currently no way to prevent this short of manually opening each routine and disabling it, then remembering to go back and re-enable each one individually later. With several routines that's tedious and error-prone (easy to forget to re-enable one).

**Proposed Solution:**
Add a single, global "Pause all routines" switch (Settings, or a toggle in the Routines list) that suspends every routine's automatic firing — including catch-up runs — without touching each task's individual `enabled` state. Flipping it back off should restore exactly what was enabled before, with no per-task bookkeeping required. This is distinct from (and complements) a per-task "skip missed runs" policy: the global pause is for "I don't want ANY routine spending tokens right now," the per-task setting is for "this specific routine's late runs are pointless."

**Alternative Solutions:**
Currently the only workaround is opening each routine and toggling `enabled: false` individually, then manually re-enabling each one later when I'm ready to resume spending on them. This doesn't scale past a couple of routines and risks forgetting to re-enable one.

**Priority:** High - Significant impact on productivity

**Feature Category:** Configuration and settings

**Use Case Example:**
1. I have several daily/weekly Routines (log checks, ads checks, etc.) that missed their slots while the app was closed.
2. I open the app while intentionally trying to conserve token usage.
3. All missed routines fire at once, consuming tokens I did not plan to spend right then.
4. With this feature, I'd flip one "pause all routines" switch before opening the app (or as soon as I notice I'm low), preventing any catch-up burst, then flip it back on later without having to remember which of my routines were enabled.

**Additional Context:**
Related to the broader missed-run/catch-up behavior discussed in #88408 and #81360, but this request is specifically about a global kill-switch for the whole routine set, not fixing catch-up logic per task."}

**What happens**

With `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/claude`, the daemon lock file is written to the configured directory, as expected, but the paths *inside* it point to the hardcoded default:

```json
// ~/.config/claude/daemon.lock
{"pid":822296,"version":"2.1.280",
 "jsonPath":"/home/<user>/.claude/daemon.json",
 "logPath":"/home/<user>/.claude/daemon.log",
 "origin":"transient","launchTarget":"/opt/bin/claude","processWrapper":"", ...}
```

So the process that honors `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` for `daemon.lock` still resolves `daemon.json` / `daemon.log` under `~/.claude`.

Probably related: after such sessions, `~/.claude/` and `~/.claude.json` reappeared in `$HOME`. `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` contained **only** trailing session metadata records (`last-prompt`, `ai-title`, `mode`, `permission-mode`, `cost-state`, `agent-name`, no messages), while the full transcripts of the same session IDs were in `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects/<slug>/`. `~/.claude/backups/.claude.json.backup.*` and `~/.claude.json` (with `projects` for the same cwd's) were written at the same times. It looks like some end-of-session / daemon code path computes the config dir without `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.

**Expected:** everything that is placed under `~/.claude` by default goes under `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when it is set, including daemon files and session metadata.

**Why it matters:** besides XDG layouts (#1455), this breaks sandboxing setups that give Claude Code a dedicated config dir: files land outside of it, and parallel sandboxed instances would share `~/.claude/daemon.json`.

Related, but different code paths: #79952 (config editing writes `~/.claude/settings.json`), #1455.

*(Written by Claude Code on the reporter's behalf.)*

{"number":97676,"title":"VS Code extension: Read/Write/Edit fail with "The user doesn't want to take this action right now" after the extension's control stream closes (no user action)","body":"**Version:** Claude Code VS Code extension 2.1.281 (bundled CLI), Linux (code-server).

**What happens**
The extension registers SDK PreToolUse hooks for `Edit|Write|Read`. When its control stream closes (chat panel or session closed while a background agent keeps running in the CLI process), every later Read/Write/Edit fails immediately (under 1 s) with:

> The user doesn't want to take this action right now. STOP what you are doing and wait for the user to tell you how to proceed.

The tool result carries `toolDenialKind: "cancelled"`. Internally the hook callback throws "Stream closed", the hook run reports "PreToolUse hook cancelled (control stream closed)", and that is mapped to the generic user-rejection text. The user did nothing. Bash, Grep and Glob are unaffected (no hook). The tool call is lost, and the model is falsely told that the user declined. In our logs the model usually continued in the same turn (83 of 83 cases on one workspace), but without the file content and with a wrong statement about the user in the transcript.

Observed: 86 cases in 14 days across 3 workspaces, 85 of them Read/Write/Edit, 72 inside background agents (sidechains), 58 under 1 s.

**Reproduction**
1. Run `claude -p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json` and register an SDK PreToolUse hook with matcher `Edit|Write|Read` over the control protocol, the same way the extension does.
2. Ask the model to run one Bash command and then read a file.
3. Close the input/control stream after the Bash call.
4. The Read fails after about 0 ms with the text above and `toolDenialKind: "cancelled"`. With the stream open, the same Read succeeds.

A real user interrupt looks different: it ends the turn and returns "doesn't want to proceed" with `error_during_execution`.

**Expected**
If the control stream for an SDK hook is closed, do not report a user rejection. Either skip the hook (fail open, as for a hook that is no longer registered) or return a distinct, truthful error such as "PreToolUse hook unavailable: control stream closed", so the agent can continue or retry. Ideally the extension deregisters its hooks when its panel closes."}

### Summary

When a **subagent** auto-compacts, the last message of the preserved segment is referenced by the compaction boundary but **never appears in the subagent's transcript**. The boundary record is the only thing on disk that mentions it.

This looks like the same writer defect as #97316 (assistant rows accumulate in memory and are not flushed after compaction). What makes it worth a separate report is the recovery condition. #97316 says:

> They appear only on a later transcript write, such as the next prompt; if nothing else happens, they are never written.

**For a subagent, "nothing else happens" is the normal case.** A subagent that compacts and then finishes its task has no later prompt, so the pending rows are never flushed and the loss is permanent. On this machine main sessions show **zero** unresolved references and subagents show **88**, which is consistent with main sessions self-healing on their next turn and subagents having no next turn.

### Evidence

`compactMetadata.preservedMessages.uuids` lists record uuids the boundary claims to have preserved. Checking each against the uuids actually present in the same transcript:

```
main      files   62  boundaries  714  unresolved preserved uuids    0  tail-identity boundaries   0
subagent  files  269  boundaries   63  unresolved preserved uuids   88  tail-identity boundaries  60
            unresolved by version: {'2.1.251': 88}
```

For **60 of the 63** subagent boundaries, the unresolved uuid is simultaneously:

- the **last** element of `compactMetadata.preservedMessages.uuids`,
- `compactMetadata.preservedSegment.tailUuid`,
- and the boundary record's own `logicalParentUuid`.

All three identical, on 60 of 60 occurrences. The remaining 28 unresolved uuids are mostly further entries in the same trailing run.

Positionally they are one slot: the following record is a `tool_result` in 696 of 696 cases, and the two surviving neighbours are adjacent lines. ### What's Wrong?

On Windows, a background subagent (auto mode, Claude Code desktop app) passed a bash script to MSYS2 inside a PowerShell double-quoted string. The script ended with rm -rf \$GNUPGHOME, meant to delete a temporary folder. PowerShell doesn't treat \$ as an escape, so it expanded $(mktemp -d) (which failed) and $GNUPGHOME (undefined, so empty). bash received rm -rf \, which MSYS2 treats as the root of the current drive. It deleted everything the user could delete from C:\ in alphabetical order, until stopped about two minutes later:

about 125 GB of personal and project folders at the drive root;
the whole working project;
files inside several installed programs (Adobe, Epic Games/Unreal, AMD and others).
Nothing went to the Recycle Bin. On an NVMe SSD with TRIM, undelete tools can't help. Recovery was only possible from a Windows shadow copy taken nine hours earlier.

Auto mode approved the command. Earlier that week, a protected-path check had blocked some PowerShell Remove-Item calls with unresolvable paths, but it didn't catch rm -rf inside a nested bash -lc "...". Closely related to #95426 (Windows, substitution resolving to a drive root, ~600 GB).

 recursive delete whose target could be empty, a variable, a subexpression, or a drive/home root should never run unattended, including when it's nested inside another shell (bash -c/-lc, sh -c, cmd /c, pwsh -Command). Treat recursive deletes in nested shells, or with variable targets, as destructive in auto mode.
Warn about PowerShell double-quoted strings containing \$ passed to a POSIX shell (a known quoting trap).
Make the sandbox the default on Windows, or strongly prompt for it.

### What's Wrong?

Title: Windows: MCP servers launched via `npx` flash a visible console window (missing windowsHide/CREATE_NO_WINDOW)

## Environment
- Claude Code (desktop app): 2.1.281, Windows
- OS: Windows 11 Enterprise 10.0.26200
- MCP servers configured in project `.mcp.json` as `"command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--cdp-endpoint", "..."]` (stdio transport)

## Description
Every time one of these `npx`-launched MCP servers starts (e.g. reconnecting a project MCP server, or opening a new session that wires up several of them), a visible, empty `cmd.exe` console window briefly (or persistently, for long-lived servers) appears on screen with a blinking cursor and no output. With several such servers configured (in our case 16 pool instances + 1 managed instance), starting/reconnecting a session can produce a burst of ~15-17 of these windows at once.

## Root cause (as far as I could trace it)
Process-tree inspection (`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`) shows the chain:


On Windows, `npx` (and the resolved package's bin script) can only be invoked through their `.cmd` shims, which requires a `cmd.exe` host process. Since `claude.exe` itself has no console, any console-subsystem child process (`cmd.exe`, and ultimately `node.exe`) that Windows creates without an explicit `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` / `windowsHide: true` spawn flag gets a brand-new, visible console window allocated for it. That flag doesn't currently appear to be set when the MCP host spawns these child processes.



## Impact
Purely cosmetic/distracting — the MCP servers function correctly, but the flashing empty console windows are confusing (easy to mistake for something else launching unexpectedly) and, with many project MCP servers configured, can produce a visible burst of windows on session start/reconnect.

Wrapping the `command` in `.mcp.json` with a hidden-window launcher (e.g. `Start-Process -WindowStyle Hidden`, or a VBScript `WScript.Shell.Run` hide trick) was considered but rejected, since those launch methods don't reliably preserve the inherited stdin/stdout pipe handles the MCP host needs for stdio transport, which would break the server's communication with the host.

### What Should Happen?

## Expected behavior
Since these are stdio-transport MCP servers (all I/O happens over pipes, not the console), no console window should ever need to be visible. The underlying Node `child_process.spawn` call should include `windowsHide: true` (which internally maps to `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`) for MCP server processes launched on Windows, regardless of whether a shell/`.cmd` shim is involved.

Auto mode has become unusable for long-running agent work since roughly 2.1.268. We run several Claude Code sessions in parallel on real engineering lanes (multi-repo PRs, deploy checks, Slack/GitHub automation). The classifier now denies ordinary, user-requested actions often enough that sessions stall partway through. Tokens are spent getting to the blocked step, and the agent then hands the human a long list of commands to run manually, which defeats the reason we run agents at all.

**There is no way to override a denial from inside the session.** The user typing "I authorize this" or "YES do it" in chat does not clear it. The denial text also forbids the agent from reaching the same outcome another way, so the only remedies are:
- stop and ask the human to run the command themselves, or
- hand-write permission rules for every new shape of command.

For us this became unbearable, so we switched `defaultMode` to `bypassPermissions` (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`). That is strictly worse for safety: we went from a model-side check that was too strict to no model-side check at all. Our own PreToolUse hooks now carry the whole load.

| Versions          | First seen         | Tool calls | Auto-mode denials | Per 1k calls |
| ----------------- | ------------------ | ---------- | ----------------- | ------------ |
| 2.1.220–2.1.250   | 2026-07-26 → 08-28 | ~13,900    | 11                | ~0.8         |

{"number":97653,"title":"Teammates inherit a stale model after refusal fallback: spawn uses the main-loop override / mainLoopModel, not the session's effective model","body":"**Version:** 2.1.280, macOS arm64. Observed on a build with unrelated local patches; no patch touches this code path.

**What happened**
1. A session on Opus 5.5 hit a `model_refusal_fallback` and was swapped to Opus 4.8.
2. About 20 minutes later the session's own turns returned to Opus 5.5: the model attachment and every assistant turn report `claude-opus-5-5`. There was no `/model`, `/clear`, resume or rewind.
3. Hours later, spawning a teammate (Agent tool, separate pane process) launched it with `--model claude-opus-4-8`. This happened both with no `model` and with an explicit `model: "opus"`.

**Expected:** the teammate runs on the lead's effective model (Opus 5.5), and `"opus"` resolves to the current Opus.

**Actual:** the teammate runs on the fallback model. From reading the bundled source:
- The refusal swap writes both the main-loop override and `AppState.mainLoopModel`. Neither is unwound until `/clear`, a rewind or a session switch.
- New turns resolve their model from `mainLoopModelForSession ?? mainLoopModel` through the runnable-model filter, which is why the session runs 5.5.
- The spawn path reads the raw override when no model is given, and the raw `mainLoopModel` when a same-family alias is given (`"opus"` -> "same family as parent, reuse the parent's model"). So it inherits the stale 4.8.
- Net effect: teammates silently run on a model the lead isn't using, even when the caller names a model family explicitly.

**Suggested fix:** have spawn inherit the same effective model that new turns use, and/or have the refusal swap's restore clear the override and `mainLoopModel` once the session stops using the fallback.

**Not determined:** what moved the session's turns back to 5.5 at step 2. The exact trigger is unknown.
"}

{"number":97652,"title":"[FEATURE] /color command: support arbitrary hex colors (terminals already support truecolor)","body":"### Preflight Checklist

- [x] I have searched [existing requests](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20label%3Aenhancement) and this feature hasn't been requested yet
- [x] This is a single feature request (not multiple features)

### Problem Statement

**Reposting https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/74447 after this was closed as "stale" which it is not.**

## Summary

The `/color` command currently accepts only 8 named colors: `red`, `blue`, `green`, `yellow`, `purple`, `orange`, `pink`, `cyan`, `default`. Modern terminals (VS Code integrated terminal, iTerm2, Ghostty, Kitty, WezTerm, Alacritty) all support 24-bit true color via `COLORTERM=truecolor`. The named-color limitation is a CLI UI decision, not a terminal constraint.

## Use case

In multi-agent projects where multiple Claude Code sessions collaborate on the same repo, each session gets a persistent identity — a name and a color stored in a project config file. The hex color is the canonical identifier used in documentation, rendered surfaces, and session provenance tracking.

The current 8-color palette forces lossy quantization: two sessions whose canonical colors are `#B45309` (amber) and `#78716C` (warm stone gray) both map to `orange`, producing a collision that defeats the purpose of per-session color identity.

## Proposed change

Accept hex colors in `/color`:

```
/color #78716C
```

**Detection**: if the argument starts with `#` and is a valid 6-digit hex color, use 24-bit ANSI escape sequences (`\033[38;2;R;G;Bm`) to render it. Named colors continue to work unchanged.

**Graceful degradation**: if `COLORTERM` is not `truecolor` or `24bit`, fall back to nearest named color (existing behavior) and optionally warn: `Terminal does not support truecolor; using nearest approximation: orange`.

## Implementation sketch

```typescript
if (arg.startsWith('#') && /^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i.test(arg)) {
  const r = parseInt(arg.slice(1,3), 16)
  const g = parseInt(arg.slice(3,5), 16)
  const b = parseInt(arg.slice(5,7), 16)
  if (process.env.COLORTERM === 'truecolor' || process.env.COLORTERM === '24bit') {
    setSessionColor(`\x1b[38;2;${r};${g};${b}m`)
  } else {
    setSessionColor(nearestNamedColor(r, g, b)) // existing fallback
  }
}
```

## Expected behavior after fix

```
/color #78716C     → session renders in warm stone gray  
/color orange      → unchanged, still works
/color #xyz        → error: "Invalid hex color"
```

## Environment

- macOS, VS Code integrated terminal + iTerm2
- `COLORTERM=truecolor` confirmed in both

{"number":97644,"title":"[BUG] Desktop: same-URL plugin MCP dedup keeps the unauthenticatable Engineering `github` server and hides the working official GitHub plugin","body":"## Summary

Two installed plugins define an MCP server with the same URL, `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`:

- **Engineering** plugin (desktop): `github` server, `type: http`, no headers (OAuth only)
- **`github@claude-plugins-official`**: `github` server, `type: http`, `Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}`

`GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` is set in the user environment and is visible to the session process. Even so, only `plugin:engineering:github` is loaded, and it stays in `needs_auth` indefinitely. `plugin:github:github` never appears in the session's server list.

The Engineering server also can't be authenticated from the desktop app: it doesn't appear in any sign-in UI, so it is stuck in `needs_auth` with no way out.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Windows 11, Claude desktop app (Code tab), Engineering plugin enabled.
2. Install and enable `github@claude-plugins-official` (user scope).
3. Set `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` as a user environment variable and fully restart the app.
4. Open a session and check the connector status.

**Actual:** `plugin:engineering:github` shows `needs_auth`, and no `plugin:github:github` server or tools are available.

**Workaround:** disable the Engineering plugin and restart. `plugin:github:github` then loads and works immediately (`get_me` succeeds).

## Expected

- When deduplicating same-URL servers, prefer the one that can authenticate (for example, one with configured headers or credentials) over an OAuth-only one that isn't signed in, **or**
- surface the conflict and let the user choose, and
- make plugin OAuth servers in `needs_auth` signable from the desktop app.

## Related

- #91847: same class of bug (same-URL dedup picks a server that cannot authenticate), headless variant
- #94321: plugin MCP OAuth in desktop sessions can't authenticate
